title: Viamonte 550 to Cornelia's Mirror: the Uncanny Life of Silvina Ocampo
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the house on Viamonte 550
stops.campa: Silvina Ocampo is born in the family house on Viamonte street, the sixth and youngest daughter of Manuel Ocampo and Ramona Aguirre, heirs of the cattle-land aristocracy of Buenos Aires province. Five older sisters already fill the house, Victoria the eldest among them; Silvina will spend her whole life named in relation to this crowded, celebrated family before she is named for herself. The century is three years old. Nothing yet marks this birth as different from any other daughter's, and everything about her later work will insist that it was.
suggested_refs: The Ocampo family's civil registry entry, Buenos Aires, 28 July 1903
sources: Fundación Konex, biographical entry
Noemí Ulla, Encuentro con Silvina Ocampo
Infobae, 'Silvina Ocampo: esa hermana menor...' (2025)

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo, the governesses' house
stops.campa: Summers are spent at Villa Ocampo, the family's house above the barranca at San Isidro, and at the city house on Viamonte; once a year the whole household, servants included, crosses to Paris. An English governess and a French one, a teacher of Castilian and one of Italian, divide Silvina's day between them, so that she learns to speak and write in English and French before she properly learns her own language. She wanders instead among the kitchens and the servants' rooms, listening to a Spanish that feels, to her, more like her own.
suggested_refs: Villa Ocampo, San Isidro, now a UNESCO World Heritage house-museum
sources: Argentina.gob.ar, 'Silvina Ocampo, 120 años de su nacimiento'
Diario de Cultura, 'A 120 años del nacimiento de Silvina Ocampo'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Viamonte 550, the death of Clara
stops.campa: From a window of the Viamonte house the sisters watch a military parade pass in the street below. Silvina turns to speak to Clara, eleven years old, and finds her face gone a strange violet color; within days the child is dead of an undiagnosed childhood diabetes. Silvina is not yet eight. The house closes briefly around this death and reopens changed: she withdraws further into the world of servants, animals, and small cruelties observed at close range, the material that will surface decades later, transposed and unforgiven, in her first book of stories.
suggested_refs: The Ocampo family plot, La Recoleta cemetery, Buenos Aires
sources: La Nación, 'Silvina Ocampo, una vida misteriosa en 10 anécdotas'
Infobae, 'Silvina Ocampo: esa hermana menor...' (2025)

stops.name: Pergamino and Villa Allende, the family's fields
stops.campa: Beyond San Isidro and the city, childhood also means the flat wheat-and-cattle land of the family's estancia near Pergamino and the sierra estate of Villa Allende in Córdoba. Here Silvina rides, watches the ranch hands work, and hears a spoken Spanish thick with turns of phrase no governess ever taught her. These fields, more than any drawing room of Sur to come, will furnish the peones, the circus folk, and the loyal, unsentimental servants who people Viaje olvidado, the book she has not yet dreamed of writing.
suggested_refs: The Ocampo family estancia lands near Pergamino, Buenos Aires province
sources: Argentina.gob.ar, 'Silvina Ocampo, 120 años de su nacimiento'
Diario de Cultura, 'A 120 años del nacimiento de Silvina Ocampo'

stops.name: Paris, arrival to study painting
stops.campa: At twenty-six, already a familiar visitor to the city from her family's yearly crossings, Silvina goes to Paris this time to study, joining the loose colony of Argentine plastic artists that calls itself the Grupo de París. She takes a studio, buys canvases, and gives herself over to drawing and painting with the seriousness her family has always reserved for marriage and land. No one in Buenos Aires yet imagines that this careful, silent girl will end her life known for sentences rather than brushstrokes.
suggested_refs: The Grupo de París roster of Argentine émigré painters, late 1920s
sources: Redbibliotecasmunicipalesgetafe.wordpress.com, '¿Quién es Silvina Ocampo?'
Artedelaargentina.com, biographical entry

stops.name: Paris, Fernand Léger's academy in Montparnasse
stops.campa: In Fernand Léger's studio-school in Montparnasse, Silvina learns the cubist discipline of planes, cylinders, and machine forms, the same rigor Léger brings to his own vast mechanical figures. She will keep, all her life, an atelier in every house she lives in, but the geometry she absorbs here will migrate, unexpectedly, into the architecture of her sentences: the flat, exact, slightly estranged way she frames a room, a face, a child's cruelty, as if composing a canvas rather than telling a story.
suggested_refs: Fernand Léger's Académie Moderne, rue Notre-Dame-des-Champs, Montparnasse
sources: Redbibliotecasmunicipalesgetafe.wordpress.com, '¿Quién es Silvina Ocampo?'
La Nación, 'Silvina Ocampo, artista visual'

stops.name: Paris, Giorgio de Chirico's lessons
stops.campa: Alongside Léger, Silvina studies with Giorgio de Chirico, founder of pittura metafisica, in his Paris rooms with their Greek profiles, arcades, and impossible shadows. Twenty years later she will fold the memory into a poem addressed to him directly, recalling the sky of Paris in his window and the columns he dreamed into paint while she, beside him, worked impetuously at her own easel. The metaphysical light he teaches her to see will resurface, transposed into prose, as the uncanny flatness of her later fiction.
stops.quote: Giorgio de Chirico, yo fui su alumna
stops.quote_source: "Epístola a Giorgio de Chirico," in Poemas de amor desesperado (1949)
suggested_refs: Giorgio de Chirico's metaphysical paintings of arcades and columns, Paris period
sources: Otra Iglesia Es Imposible, 'Silvina Ocampo / Epístola a Giorgio de Chirico'
Auster, 'El mundo clásico en la poesía de Silvina Ocampo'

stops.name: Paris, exhibiting with the Grupo de París
stops.campa: She shows drawings and paintings alongside the other Argentine expatriates of the Grupo de París in the small Montparnasse galleries that host them. It is respectable, competent work, and it is not, she is beginning to suspect, the place where her real strangeness lives. Something in the discipline of the brush keeps the cruelty and the wonder of her childhood at arm's length; only sentences, she will later imply, let her get close enough to the thing itself to frighten herself with it.
suggested_refs: Grupo de París group exhibitions, Montparnasse galleries, c. 1930
sources: Artedelaargentina.com, biographical entry
Redbibliotecasmunicipalesgetafe.wordpress.com, '¿Quién es Silvina Ocampo?'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the slow abandonment of painting
stops.campa: Back in Buenos Aires, Silvina keeps a studio in the family houses, as she will for the rest of her life, but the balance is already tipping: she begins trying sentences the way she once tried compositions, in secret, without showing them. Her sister Victoria's world of writers, translators, and literary reviews surrounds her at every family lunch. The painter does not yet know she is about to become, instead, one of the strangest prose stylists of her language.
suggested_refs: Silvina Ocampo's studio, kept in every house she later lived in
sources: La Nación, 'Silvina Ocampo, artista visual'
Perfil, 'Silvina Ocampo: la cuentista que quería conmover'

segments.name: Sur, Rincón Viejo, and the Meeting of the Three

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo — the founding of Sur
stops.campa: Victoria launches the review Sur from the family house at San Isidro, meaning to open Argentina onto world letters and the world onto Argentina, with Ortega y Gasset and Waldo Frank among its advisory names. Silvina, the youngest sister, watches the court of poets and translators her sister has assembled fill the same rooms where she once hid from governesses. She is not yet a contributor. But the circle that will make her a writer, and introduce her to the two men who will define the rest of her life, is already gathering here.
suggested_refs: Sur magazine no. 1, January 1931, founded by Victoria Ocampo
borges.journey.json (shared pin, the same founding)
sources: Sur magazine, no. 1 (1931)
borges.journey.json (shared pin)

stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Ocampo — meeting Bioy Casares
stops.campa: Through their mutual friend Borges, Silvina, thirty, meets Adolfo Bioy Casares, nineteen, at one of Victoria's gatherings at Villa Ocampo, the same house, the same year almost, where Borges himself met Bioy the season before. The age gap scandalizes no one yet, because nothing has happened yet to scandalize; only later will the eleven years between them, and her refusal to explain herself to anyone, become part of the family's private legend of Silvina as the difficult, unclassifiable sister.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the young Bioy Casares and Silvina Ocampo, early 1930s
borges.journey.json (shared pin, Borges meeting Bioy the year before)
sources: Billiken, 'Amores históricos: Adolfo Bioy Casares y Silvina Ocampo'
Diario Hoy, 'Adolfo Bioy Casares y Silvina Ocampo: una historia de amor turbulenta'

stops.name: Rincón Viejo, Pardo — the house where she begins to write
stops.campa: Silvina and Adolfo begin living together, unmarried, at Rincón Viejo, the Bioy family's English-style estancia near the village of Pardo, in the district of Las Flores, a arrangement unheard of for a woman of her class and age. It is here, by Bioy's own account, that she sets aside brush and canvas and starts, in earnest, to write: the stories that will become Viaje olvidado take shape in this pampa quiet. Borges visits often; the friendship of the three, which will outlast every scandal, consolidates on this same veranda.
suggested_refs: Estancia Rincón Viejo, Pardo, Las Flores, Buenos Aires province
sources: Noticias Las Flores, 'Pardo, el pueblo donde Bioy Casares y Borges encontraron inspiración'
La Nación, 'Adolfo Bioy Casares: viaje al corazón de su obra'

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Viaje olvidado published
stops.campa: Sur, her own sister's press, publishes Silvina's first book: twenty-eight stories of circus performers, governesses, sick children, and unswervingly loyal servants, drawn from the same nurseries and service quarters of her own childhood. It passes almost unnoticed. Borges, reading her prose for the first time as a body of work, will later name the trait in it that unsettles him most: a strange love for an innocent, or oblique, cruelty he cannot quite account for.
stops.quote: Hay un rasgo que aún no he llegado a comprender bien: cierto extraño amor por la crueldad inocente, o si se quiere, oblicua.
stops.quote_source: Jorge Luis Borges, on the prose of Silvina Ocampo
suggested_refs: Viaje olvidado, first edition, Sur, Buenos Aires, 1937
sources: Viaje olvidado, Wikipedia (es)
El Historiador, 'La prosa de Silvina Ocampo, por Jorge Luis Borges'

stops.name: Las Flores — the marriage to Bioy Casares
stops.campa: After six years together at Rincón Viejo, Silvina and Adolfo marry at the civil registry of Las Flores, Borges among the witnesses alongside Óscar Pardo and Enrique Drago Mitre. There is no party, no celebration, little more than a formality after so long an informal life; she is thirty-six, he twenty-five. The marriage that follows will run more than fifty years, unconventional to the end, each of them keeping rooms, hours, and, in his case, other loves the other learns to hold at a private distance.
suggested_refs: The civil registry marriage record, Las Flores, 15 January 1940
sources: Las Flores municipal site, 'El día que Bioy Casares se casó en Las Flores con Borges como testigo'
Cervantes Virtual, wedding photograph archive

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Antología de la literatura fantástica published
stops.campa: Silvina, Borges, and Bioy Casares publish together, through Sudamericana, an anthology of fantastic tales gathered from ancient China to contemporary England and France, Kafka, Chesterton, Cocteau, Dunany, Poe among them. Bioy signs the modest prologue for all three. It is the first time the three names appear bound together on a title page, an emblem of the alliance of taste and friendship that will outlast, in print, nearly everything else that happens to any of them.
stops.quote: Este volumen es, simplemente, la reunión de los textos de la literatura fantástica que nos parecen mejores.
stops.quote_source: Adolfo Bioy Casares, prólogo to Antología de la literatura fantástica (1940)
suggested_refs: Antología de la literatura fantástica, first edition, Sudamericana, 1940
sources: Antología de la literatura fantástica, Borges Center bibliography
Ciudad Seva, 'Prólogo a la Antología de la literatura fantástica'

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Enumeración de la patria, Borges' review
stops.campa: Her first book of poems recovers the old Castilian meters to enumerate the rivers, saints' days, and cattle-land of Argentina itself, the country of her own family's estancias turned into verse. Borges reviews it in Sur, comparing the new poet to Whitman, the first public crowning of Silvina as a writer in her own right rather than merely someone's sister, someone's friend, and soon, someone's wife.
suggested_refs: Enumeración de la patria, first edition, Sur, 1942
sources: La biblioteca de Marcelo Leites, 'Enumeración de la patria'
Escritores.org, biographical entry

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Espacios métricos and the Premio Municipal
stops.campa: A second collection of verse, its very title borrowed from the language of geometry she learned from Léger, measures stanzas the way she once measured a canvas. It wins the Premio Municipal de Poesía, the city of Buenos Aires formally recognizing what her family and her closest readers already knew: whatever else she is, she is now, undeniably, a poet.
suggested_refs: Espacios métricos, first edition, 1945
sources: Fundación Konex, biographical entry
Escritores.org, biographical entry

stops.name: Mar del Plata — writing Los que aman, odian with Bioy
stops.campa: At the end of summer, by the sea, Silvina and Adolfo write a detective novel together in a little over a month, inventing episodes between them and recognizing at once, without argument, which sentence is the right one. It becomes Los que aman, odian, a poisoning at a solitary beach hotel, the only novel the two of them will ever sign jointly, proof, Bioy will say, that Silvina's originality was inevitable and that working beside her was nothing but a pleasure.
stops.quote: Nunca hubo una discusión ni una pelea con Silvina: inventábamos episodios, alguien proponía una solución y yo escribía... la aceptábamos sin discusiones.
stops.quote_source: Adolfo Bioy Casares, on writing Los que aman, odian (1946)
suggested_refs: Los que aman, odian, first edition, El Séptimo Círculo, Emecé, 1946
sources: La Prensa Panamá, 'Bioy Casares y Silvina Ocampo, a dúo en Los que aman, odian'
Infobae, 'Los que aman, odian: una trama de intriga, celos y amores no correspondidos'

segments.name: Autobiografía de Irene and the Cruel Tales

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Autobiografía de Irene published
stops.campa: Five stories, the title piece narrated by Irene Andrade, a young woman cursed to see the future while she forgets the past entirely, memory itself doubled and inverted, the fantastic turned inward as a psychological condition rather than an external marvel. It is the clearest early statement of the device Silvina will use for the rest of her career: the uncanny not as intrusion from outside but as the ordinary shape of a mind examining itself.
suggested_refs: Autobiografía de Irene, first edition, Sudamericana, 1948
sources: Un libro al día, 'Silvina Ocampo: Autobiografía de Irene'
Caravana de recuerdos, 'Autobiografía de Irene'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Posadas 1650 — Marta, the given daughter
stops.campa: In the United States, one of Bioy's lovers gives birth to his daughter, Marta. Silvina, fifty and childless, receives the infant into the marriage at the family's Recoleta apartment and adopts her formally as her own, overprotecting the girl for the rest of her life. It is a private act of grief and generosity the public Sur circle rarely mentions, hidden the way most of the real weather of this marriage stays hidden behind its literary partnership.
suggested_refs: The Bustillo-designed apartment building, Posadas 1650, Recoleta, Buenos Aires
sources: Tumblr, 'Marta Bioy Ocampo era la hija de Bioy Casares y hija adoptiva de Silvina Ocampo'
Diario Hoy, 'Adolfo Bioy Casares y Silvina Ocampo: una historia de amor turbulenta'

stops.name: Buenos Aires — La furia published
stops.campa: The collection critics later call the one that ferociously inaugurates her true narrative voice: a golden hare, a jealousy monologue turning in on itself without end, ordinary households harboring an evil no one names directly. The oblique cruelty Borges noticed in her first book, twenty years earlier, is now fully unsheathed, deliberate, and entirely her own instrument.
suggested_refs: La furia, first edition, Sur, 1959
sources: Google Books, La furia by Silvina Ocampo
Un libro al día, entries on Silvina Ocampo's story collections

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Las invitadas published
stops.campa: Thirty stories of women and girls, small thefts of identity, guests who never quite belong in the houses that contain them. Reviewers will later read the title as a private joke: Silvina herself has spent thirty years being introduced in other people's houses as somebody's sister, somebody's wife, somebody's friend, never quite at home under her own name.
suggested_refs: Las invitadas, first edition, Sur, 1961
sources: Fundación Konex, biographical entry
GradeSaver, Silvina Ocampo biography and works

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Alejandra Pizarnik at Sara Facio's studio
stops.campa: At the photographer Sara Facio's studio, the young poet Alejandra Pizarnik, sitting for a portrait, loses the composed persona she has built the instant Silvina walks into the room. Over the years that follow Pizarnik writes her six letters of admiration, confidence, and increasingly desperate affection, calling her a lost paradise; Silvina answers with the same careful, unhurried reserve she gives everyone, a kindness that will not, in the end, be quite enough.
stops.quote_source: Alejandra Pizarnik, letter to Silvina Ocampo, c. 1969-1972 (published correspondence)
suggested_refs: Sara Facio's photographic portraits of Silvina Ocampo and Alejandra Pizarnik
The letters of Alejandra Pizarnik to Silvina Ocampo, 1969-1972
sources: Medium, 'Silvina Ocampo y Alejandra Pizarnik: historia de un amor inconcluso'
Infobae, 'La última carta de Pizarnik a Ocampo'

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Lo amargo por dulce published
stops.campa: A book of poems whose title turns a proverb inside out, bitterness disguised as sweetness, the same device she has used in prose for twenty-five years now given fully to verse: nursery rhyme meters carrying an adult's dread, comfort words holding something that does not comfort at all. Critics reaching for her in this decade still default to describing her as Bioy's wife or Borges's friend; the poems themselves, read closely, answer that condescension by refusing every consoling cliché of domestic verse from the inside.
suggested_refs: Lo amargo por dulce, first edition, 1962
sources: Escritores.org, biographical entry
Fundación Konex, biographical entry

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Los días de la noche published
stops.campa: Day and night reversed in the very title, doubling again the device that has carried her whole career. The stories increasingly turn to children as clear-eyed witnesses of an adult cruelty and an adult magic that, from where a child stands, look exactly alike. She is sixty-seven now, still keeping her own hours apart from Bioy's, still writing in the mornings in the same unhurried, exact prose she brought back from Léger's geometry forty years before, in a studio in Paris she rarely mentions anymore.
suggested_refs: Los días de la noche, first edition, 1970
sources: GradeSaver, Silvina Ocampo biography and works
Fundación Konex, biographical entry

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Amarillo celeste published
stops.campa: A collection of poems named for Argentina's own colors, inverted: sky-blue turned yellow, the flag's calm undone into something stranger. Forty years after Chirico's Paris rooms, it is her own private metaphysical light, oblique and muted, answering the columns and shadows she once learned to paint rather than to write. She is nearly seventy, still publishing steadily, still overshadowed in the daily papers by her sister's foundation and her husband's growing international fame, and entirely unconcerned by either.
suggested_refs: Amarillo celeste, first edition, 1972
sources: Escritores.org, biographical entry
Fundación Konex, biographical entry

stops.name: Buenos Aires — the Konex award
stops.campa: The Fundación Konex names her among the essential short-story writers of the decade, a public honor arriving late in a life spent being introduced, first, as someone else's relation. She accepts it the way she accepts most public things now: politely, briefly, and without any wish to explain herself further to a country only beginning to read her on her own terms.
suggested_refs: Fundación Konex Diploma al Mérito, Cuento, 1984
sources: Fundación Konex, biographical entry

stops.name: Madrid — La torre sin fin published
stops.campa: Alfaguara publishes, almost in secret, her last book for children: Leandro's dream-journey through impossible climates and a confrontation with the Devil, a rite of passage narrated with the same resplendent, untroubled prose she gave her cruelest adult stories. The book is barely distributed in Argentina and will not be properly known there for another two decades.
suggested_refs: La torre sin fin, first edition, Alfaguara, Madrid, 1986, illustrated by Gogo Husso
sources: Eterna Cadencia, 'La torre sin fin'
Lecturalia, 'La torre sin fin'

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Y así sucesivamente published
stops.campa: A late collection whose very title shrugs at continuity, fantastic beings still breeding inside perfectly ordinary sentences. Almost no one around her yet says the word aloud, but the first symptoms of the illness that will end her working life are already beginning to show themselves in these last, still perfectly controlled pages. She is eighty-four, still writing every morning at Posadas 1650, still receiving Bioy's friends and hers for the lunches that have gone on, almost unbroken, for sixty years.
suggested_refs: Y así sucesivamente, first edition, 1987
sources: Fundación Konex, biographical entry
GradeSaver, Silvina Ocampo biography and works

stops.name: Buenos Aires — Cornelia frente al espejo, the mirror's verdict
stops.campa: Her last book of stories, populated by doubles, reflections, and fantastic creatures seen through the distorting eyes of their own narrators, wins the Premio Club de los XIII. In this same year Alzheimer's disease begins visibly to take hold. The mirror of the title becomes, without anyone intending it, her final self-portrait: the spectator of herself, as she has always called it, about to lose the name for what she is watching.
stops.quote: No soy sociable, soy íntima. Soy apenas yo misma. Soy Silvina. Fui y soy la espectadora de mí misma.
stops.quote_source: Silvina Ocampo, interview with Noemí Ulla, in Encuentro con Silvina Ocampo
suggested_refs: Cornelia frente al espejo, first edition, Tusquets, 1988
sources: Internet Archive, Cornelia frente al espejo
El Destape, 'A 28 años de la muerte de Silvina Ocampo: No soy sociable, soy íntima'

stops.name: San Isidro — the years of the illness
stops.campa: Bedridden now in the family house at San Isidro, Silvina's Alzheimer's has taken most of the exact names she once distributed so carefully among her characters. Bioy, past seventy, cares for a wife who no longer always recognizes him, the long unconventional marriage of fifty years closing in almost exactly the register it began: patient, unexplained, conducted mostly in silence and in service.
suggested_refs: The Ocampo-Bioy family house, San Isidro, her last residence
sources: Cadena 3, 'Silvina Ocampo, la eterna hermana menor'
El Destape, 'A 28 años de la muerte de Silvina Ocampo'

stops.name: San Isidro — the death
stops.campa: Silvina Ocampo dies at ninety, three years bedridden, in the San Isidro house. Twenty days later her adopted daughter Marta is killed by a car in Buenos Aires, a second loss closing, almost too cruelly for even her own fiction, the household Bioy built around this fifty-three-year marriage. Borges has been dead seven years; only Bioy remains of the three names bound together on the 1940 anthology's title page.
suggested_refs: Silvina Ocampo's grave, La Recoleta cemetery, Buenos Aires
sources: La Nación, 'Genialidad y bizarrismo: treinta años sin Silvina Ocampo'
Tumblr, 'Marta Bioy Ocampo era la hija de Bioy Casares'

stops.name: Buenos Aires — La promesa and the canon's verdict
stops.campa: La promesa, the novel Silvina carried unfinished for over a decade, dictating fragments during the failing years before her diagnosis, is finally published nearly two decades after her death. Read now apart from her sister's fame and her husband's and her closest friend's, she is named at last, by the readers of a new generation, the strangest of the whole Sur circle, the one who saw furthest into the ordinary cruelty of houses, mirrors, and the people who keep them.
suggested_refs: La promesa, posthumous edition, Buenos Aires, 2011
sources: Letras Libres, 'Silvina Ocampo: el etcétera de la familia'
The Objective, 'Silvina Ocampo, mucho más que la hermana menor'
